title: ECB Holds Rates Steady but Signals September Hike as Middle East Conflict Drives Energy Prices Higher
excerpt: The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.25% on Thursday, but President Christine Lagarde signaled the door remains open to further tightening as oil prices climb above $100 a barrel.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The ECB maintained its deposit rate at 2.25%, pausing after a June hike.
  • Markets anticipate two more quarter-point increases by year-end, with September likely.
  • Oil prices surged above $100 due to the U.S.-Iran conflict, raising inflation risks.
  • Germany's 10-year bond yield reached 3.2%, the highest since 2011.

ECB Pauses After June Hike

The European Central Bank held its benchmark deposit rate at 2.25% on Thursday, pausing after its first rate increase in nearly three years last month. The decision, widely anticipated by markets, came as the central bank weighs the competing pressures of a fragile economic recovery and an energy shock that refuses to fade.

In its statement, the ECB said it was "closely monitoring the intensity and duration of the shock, as well as its indirect and second-round effects," adding that the outlook for energy prices "currently stands close to the baseline of the June Eurosystem staff projections and well above levels recorded prior to the conflict in the Middle East."

The main refinancing rate and marginal lending facility rate remained at 2.40% and 2.65%, respectively.

Lagarde Keeps September in Play

At her press conference, ECB President Christine Lagarde revealed that some governing council members had pushed for an immediate rate increase.

"There were some governors who asked themselves whether we should not consider a hike. We all unanimously decided that we were positioned adequately to wait."

— Christine Lagarde, ECB President

That language keeps the September 9-10 meeting firmly live. Derivatives markets are pricing in nearly two more quarter-point hikes by the end of 2026, with Bank of America explicitly forecasting a September increase. ING strategist Francesco Pesole noted that a surprise hike at this meeting "should not be fully ruled out," while Citigroup economists said they "still envisage another rate hike before the year-end."

Energy Shock Returns

The collapse of the U.S.-Iran ceasefire in mid-June has reshaped the inflation outlook. Oil prices have jumped back above $100 a barrel as U.S. strikes on Iran entered their twelfth consecutive day, disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude has risen 22% in one month, according to MarketWatch, while West Texas Intermediate surged nearly 8% in a single session this week.

Eurozone inflation cooled to 2.8% in June from 3.2% in May, offering temporary relief. But Lagarde warned that higher energy costs have already bled into other sectors, particularly transportation, and that policymakers are closely watching for second-round effects such as wage pressures.

"We are concerned, which leads us to being very attentive. We are not at that stage where we are seeing those signs of second-round effects."

— Christine Lagarde, ECB President

Bond Markets Flash Warning Signs

European government borrowing costs have climbed to their highest levels in more than a decade. Germany's 10-year bond yield reached 3.2% this week — a level last seen in 2011 — while France's benchmark yield topped 4% for the first time since 2009, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The euro fell 0.2% to $1.1388 following the decision, and two-year German bond yields rose roughly 2 basis points to 2.86%, according to Reuters.

Madison Faller, global investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Private Bank, said policymakers would need energy prices to "roll over quickly" and see "little sign of spillover into the broader economy" to justify holding rates in September — "conditions that look increasingly difficult to meet."

ECB Leads Among G7 Central Banks

The ECB remains the only G7 central bank to have raised rates since the Middle East conflict escalated in late February. The Federal Reserve, Bank of England, and Bank of Canada all held steady in their most recent meetings, though traders are betting both the Fed and BOE could begin hiking in the coming months. The Bank of Japan hiked separately in June to 1%, its highest rate since 1995.

Analysts at Bank of America struck a longer-term note of caution, writing that "irrespective of whether the ECB hikes once or twice this year, policy rates at the end of 2027 will be 2% at most," arguing that inflation will prove less persistent than feared and that the current energy shock is "nowhere near that of 2022."

Lagarde also quashed speculation about an early departure, saying she plans to serve through at least the end of 2027. "When there are clouds on the horizon, the captain stays on the ship," she said.
